extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional scholars, and policymakers interested in parliamentary/cabinet government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the conditions and institutional criteria the essay identifies as necessary for effective cabinet (parliamentary) government, with English-specific examples and proposed legal safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual confidence of the electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The first prerequisite of elective government is the MUTUAL CONFIDENCE of the electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay stresses that electors must trust one another to choose representatives; without diffuse credit in fellow citizens the indirect processes of representative government cannot function. Lack of trust (diffused distrust and indiscriminate suspicion) prevents concerted co-operation between regions and undermines the choice of executive rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm national mind (stability to bear revolutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A CALM national mind—a tone of mind sufficiently stable to bear the necessary excitement of conspicuous revolutions—is required for elective government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semi-civilised or excitable populations cannot be entrusted with elections without risk of violent usurpation. The presence of august institutions (e.g., a monarch) helps by providing an appearance of continuity that prevents mass excitement. Anti-pattern: sudden, large-scale popular excitement where people cannot distinguish 'reigning' from 'governing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationality (capacity to conceive distant objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: RATIONALITY: a power involving intelligence that enables the populace to form distinct conceptions of distant or abstract political objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electors must be able to understand and deliberate about remote/institutional matters; without this capacity the system of electing rulers is impracticable. This differs from mere intelligence: it is the civic ability to treat abstract constitutional distinctions as real and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a competent, continuous legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet government requires a legislature not only to exist continuously but to be competent—willing and able to elect and maintain an efficient executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A permanent, actively functioning legislature that can make and unmake laws is essential. Historical contrast: early societies valued fixed, unchanging law and would find continuous legislatures anomalous. Modern civilised states need an 'adjusting legislation' to adapt laws to changing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient substantial business for Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: To keep a legislature efficient it must have a sufficient supply of substantial business; without it Members will quarrel about little and produce feeble administrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Parliament has too little non-elective business, controversies about ministries will dominate and small factions will proliferate. The essay warns that a Parliament with little to do must be intrinsically excellent or it will fail; substantial affairs steady and improve otherwise indifferent parliaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: A population that is educated and comfortable
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation whose mass of people are intelligent and comfortable (diffused education and absence of 'honest poverty') can elect a good Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New England-style communities where education and comfort are widespread produce electorates capable of choosing competent legislatures. Conversely, poverty and ignorance make electing a competent legislature difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical conditions: population density and compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical dispersion (sparse or scattered population) impedes discussion and makes forming a competent legislature more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, sparsely populated countries face obstacles in communication and deliberation; this practical difficulty can hinder the functioning of Cabinet government even where the populace is otherwise fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early social equality aids initial cabinet government in colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: In early agricultural colonies, a practical social equality (absence of entrenched classes) makes Cabinet government conceivable because equality establishes itself naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that initial social democracy in colonies helps the formation of competent legislatures, though over time inequality and class differentiation can complicate matters. Example anecdote: settlers in Western Australia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative willingness to elect and maintain an efficient executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond structural competence, a legislature must be willing to elect and maintain an efficient executive (i.e., supply stable administrations long enough to prove their sufficiency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabinet government depends on both getting a good legislature and keeping it good. Failing to maintain stable administrations leads to a succession of feeble ministries—contrary to the aims of cabinet government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premier-controlled ordinary peer-creation to harmonise the Upper House
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary, continual power to create peers (a few year by year) is best exercised by the Premier as head of the predominant party to modify the House of Lords gradually to suit public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gradual appointments allow the responsible executive to harmonise the revising chamber with the legislature and public opinion. The essay argues hardly any constitution provides such a delicate and flexible machinery for modifying a secondary chamber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catastrophic peer-creation reserved for great occasions and impartial hands
rubrics_metrics.description: The catastrophic power to create many peers (to 'swamp' the Upper House) is a power only to be used on great occasions, and, ideally, in the hands of an able and impartial monarch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reserve power should be sparingly used to resolve immense objectives when party strife is unmitigated. If available, an impartial monarch could prevent years of tumult; but the rarity of such monarchs makes its placement problematic. Anti-pattern: capricious or partisan use of mass creations (e.g., Queen Anne's caprice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrusting extreme constitutional powers to hereditary sovereigns is risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting critical and extreme constitutional force to hereditary sovereigns is dangerous because the quality (ability, impartiality) of monarchs is unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Queen Anne, William IV, George III) show weak or capricious monarchs can misuse or fail to use such powers, producing crises. Thus reliance on hereditary occupants for decisive interventions is insecure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferential placement of dissolution and reserve checks in the Premier rather than the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The check of possible dissolution and similar executive reserves are better placed in the Premier than the sovereign under modern British practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues the Premier is a better locus for dissolution power because the sovereign's intervention historically hurt rather than helped true party principles; practice has concentrated this check in the Premier to Parliament's advantage. Example: sovereigns refusing dissolution or exercising it inconsistently created crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional/legal safeguard proposal for extraordinary peer-creation
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed legal safeguard: prevent creation of an extraordinary number of peers (e.g., more than ten annually) except upon a large parliamentary majority (suggested three-fourths of the Lower House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory restriction would ensure the Premier could not expend the reserve force as an ordinary administrative power and would reserve it for a genuine revolution supported by the nation. It is offered to illustrate a institutional design remedy to the unpredictability of hereditary sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions in new states must show obvious, conspicuous utility
rubrics_metrics.description: New communities must choose governments and institutions that demonstrate obvious, evident utility; forms like ceremonial royalty are often unconvincing to prosaic, utility-oriented colonial minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that settlers shaped by struggle with the wilderness value visible, demonstrable results; constitutional royalty (mystery and ceremonial function) is less likely to command loyalty in colonies, which prefer institutions with clear practical benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public preference for visible results (matter-of-factness) influences acceptable institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'matter-of-fact' public mindset that judges institutions by results rather than abstract ideas shapes what political forms are practicable and respected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include modern commerce and physical science promoting a stock-taking habit: citizens ask 'what have you done since I saw you last?' Governments and offices that produce observable utility win respect; those that don't will be dismissed by such publics.
